Q: Keep old TabView style in iOS / iPadOS 18.1 A:

Update: This no longer works as of iOS 26.4

---

You can call this method at the start of your app lifecycle (in SwiftUI you'd need to use an App Delegate depending on how early your tab bar view appears):

UserDefaults.standard.register(defaults: ["UseFloatingTabBar": false])

This will give you the old-style tab bar. On iOS 18 it will stretch across the device (like it used to on iOS 17) but on iOS 26 it will be only as wide as it needs to be.

This also works with modern tab bar features such as the separate inline search.

This is an internal flag within the system similar to defaults write on macOS. That means it is officially unsupported and could be removed in a future version of iPadOS but the risks are manageable. I have used it in several production apps since the launch of iPadOS 18 in 2024 and have never had any issues with App Review. The fact that they redesigned this component for Liquid Glass makes me fairly confident it won’t be removed anytime soon.

-- https://bendodson.com/weblog/2026/01/22/traditional-tab-bar-on-ipados-26/

Q: Attach to a container + auto install plugins A:

There is no VS Code setting or configuration that allows automatic installation of extension. There is however the possibility to recommend extensions, on a workspace/folder level, and VS Code will display a notification about it.

To accomplish this, create a file .vscode/extensions.json with something like this:

{
  "recommendations": [
    "ms-python.python",
    "esbenp.prettier-vscode",
    "dbaeumer.vscode-eslint"
  ]
}

On the other hand, if you are dealing with docker-compose, you could use the VS Code CLI and install the extensions via shell, using the --install-extension arg. More details in https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/editor/command-line#_working-with-extensions


You can list extensions currently installed by running the following command in the VS Code Terminal

code --list-extensions

Q: How to avoid repeatedly passing a string slice to helper method without adding lifetime? A:

You underestimate the cost of refactoring of badly designed code. Replacing ref count with lifetime managed references will almost always mean huge refactoring. On the other hand once you learn lifetimes there is no significant development cost to it. Or at least I don't see it. You just need a different mindset.

Q: ARM Literal Pool definition in a mixed C and assembly function A:

There may be the frame pointer register (R13 is the stack pointer, not the frame pointer), but the compiler by default does not use it for this purpose. Everything is done via SP, which changes with PUSH/POP, causing wrong code to be generated should you PUSH or POP yourself. Note that you cannot use R13 as an index register on ARMv6-M anyway, so using the frame pointer is kind of slow and stupid.

That said, the kind of self test you want to do is sensible, but I strongly recommend you do it using assembly in an assembly source file, not inline assembly. There is no good way to use GNU inline assembly for what you want to do. If you do foolishly decide to use inline assembly, do pay attention to register asm("...") variables for when you want to tie variables to specific registers.
